cells.tense: You are here with the pen, gathering the scattered lines into one coherent order.
cells.act: let the inner compass decide the small case
cells.ask: When a small choice about your practice comes up — which drill, how long, whether to repeat it — let your own sense of what's right settle it once. Don't reopen it after.
cells.core:
Your practice has become a place where the pieces come together. Lines that ran loose all day get collected here — what happened, what it meant, what to do next — and the bench is where they settle into one order. That exchange is fair to you: you give the work your attention, and it hands back a clearer head. Nothing about it needs an audit.

The good state holds because you aren't arguing with yourself while you work. Trust your own read on the small calls from here — which drill to run, how long to stay — and stand behind the choice instead of relitigating it halfway through. The session gets to be one thing rather than a debate. What you'll have is a practice that keeps going without you refereeing it, and a head that stays gathered after you leave.

cells.tense: You will have the whole session planned before you sit down, and the plan will be the work.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Take one piece of your practice at the pace a month would allow rather than a day — one rep, one page, one pass — then stop there on purpose.
cells.core:
Ahead of every session there's a plan for the session, and the plan keeps growing. Everything gets gathered into a strategy before your hands have touched anything, and the strategy is so complete that the work itself arrives as an afterthought. You're bracing for a version of this that hasn't happened yet — the perfect run, the breakthrough — and the bench waits while the outline gets redrawn.

What's thin here isn't discipline. It's contact. Take one piece at the pace a month would allow rather than a day, and the doing will tell you what the plan couldn't. The gathering still happens; it just happens in your hands, at the speed of real work, where it can be revised. What you'll have is a practice that moves and a head that stops rehearsing tomorrow.

cells.tense: You were at the bench once, and you keep standing at the door of it.
cells.act: spend an hour with the thing you love without a task attached to it
cells.ask: Give an hour to the part of your practice you actually love — the instrument, the page, the movement — with no drill and no goal attached.
cells.core:
The bench is behind you now. Lines still get gathered, but they get gathered somewhere else — in the planning, in the remembering of when this went well, in the version you keep meaning to return to. The sessions don't happen, and the not-happening has its own low hum. What's left is a door you've already walked through, still being stood at.

Don't force the drill. Go back through the feeling instead: an hour with the part of this you actually love, no task on it, nothing to produce. Your heart already knows what it knows about this work — let that be what carries you back to the bench. What you'll have is the pull, felt again, before any of the doing.

cells.tense: You are already at the bench now, gathering the lines, and calling it just how practice goes.
cells.act: mark the good thing together, the day it happens
cells.ask: When your practice goes well, tell the person who'd want to know — the one who asks — before it cools into a private fact.
cells.core:
The gathering is happening in your hands right now — collecting the lines into one clear order, quietly, session after session. Asked about it, you'd say the work speaks for itself, or that this is simply what showing up looks like. Somebody is running this, and that somebody doesn't get named.

The piece that's missing is the telling. When a session goes well, it stays with you alone, private, uncounted. Say it out loud to the person who asks — the one who'd want to know — the same day, before the glow fades into a fact. The practice gets a witness, and you get to see your own hand in it. That's the whole change: the making gets said.
